title: Idioms, slang and regional speech
objectives: I can understand common Brazilian slang, fillers and idioms in relaxed conversation.
I can recognize regional words and accents from the Southeast, Minas Gerais, the Northeast and the South.
I can use discourse markers such as tipo, né, aí and sei lá to sound natural in informal speech.
I can tell slang apart from vulgar language and from formal register, and choose the right one for the situation.

vocabulary.note: Usage: a filler that introduces an example or softens a statement. The same word is the ordinary noun o tipo, 'the type' or 'the kind' (um tipo de música, a kind of music); as a filler it is used as if to say 'a sort of thing, such as'. Spelling and sound: t before i says ch, so it is CHEE-poo; the final o is a short u; the stress is on the second to last syllable, the default for an ending in o, so no mark is written.

example.target: Tipo, eu nem sabia que ele ia viajar.
example.source: Like, I did not even know he was going to travel.
example.source_literal: Type, I not-even knew that he was-going to-travel.

vocabulary.note: Usage: a tag question that asks the listener to agree, and also a filler. It is não é, 'not is', said so fast that the nasal vowel of não is lost. Spelling and sound: one syllable, stressed, ending in e, so it takes a mark; the vowel is the open e of é, so the mark is the acute. The weak word e, 'and', has no mark.

example.target: Tá frio hoje, né?
example.source: It is cold today, isn't it?
example.source_literal: Is cold today, not-is?

vocabulary.note: Usage: a mild exclamation of surprise or complaint, very common in Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo. It is a softened form of a stronger vulgar word, which is why it is informal but harmless. It has no literal meaning, so there is no literal gloss. Spelling and sound: one stressed syllable ending in o, so it takes a mark; the vowel is the closed o of English go without the glide, so the mark is the circumflex.

example.target: Pô, você podia ter avisado!
example.source: Gosh, you could have let me know!
example.source_literal: Pô, you could have warned!

vocabulary.note: Usage: used to address a friend of any gender, or to say 'guy' (o cara, the guy). The feminine noun a cara is 'the face'; the masculine o cara, 'the guy', is a separate use of the same word, so the gender changes with the meaning. Spelling and sound: c before a is k; the r between vowels is a tap; the stress is on the second to last syllable, so no mark.

example.target: Cara, você viu o jogo ontem?
example.source: Dude, did you see the game yesterday?
example.source_literal: Face, you saw the game yesterday?

vocabulary.note: Usage: typical of São Paulo. It is a clipped form of irmão, 'brother'. In Rio the equivalent is mermão, which is meu irmão, 'my brother', run together. Spelling and sound: the n between vowels is an ordinary n; the stress is on ma, the default for an ending in o. In mermão the ão is a stressed nasal ending, as in pão, and the rm is an r closing the syllable (its sound varies by region) followed by m.

example.target: Mano, esse filme é muito bom.
example.source: Bro, this movie is really good.
example.source_literal: Brother, this film is very good.

vocabulary.note: Usage: a casual way to express uncertainty or indifference, close to 'I have no idea'. Lá is 'there', which adds a sense of distance, as if to say 'how would I know, that is over there'. Spelling and sound: sei has the diphthong ei, which is one beat, like English 'say' with a short glide; lá is a stressed one-syllable word ending in a, so it takes the acute (the open a).

example.target: Sei lá, acho que ele esqueceu.
example.source: I don't know, I think he forgot.
example.source_literal: I-know there, I-think that he forgot.

vocabulary.note: Usage: agrees with what was said, often with a tone of resignation, and can also open an explanation. Pois usually means 'since' or 'because' as a conjunction, but here it has lost that sense and only links the phrase to the previous speaker. Spelling and sound: pois has the diphthong oi; its final s is s in São Paulo and sh in Rio. É is the stressed one-syllable word with the open e, so it has the acute.

example.target: Pois é, a reunião foi cancelada de novo.
example.source: Yeah, the meeting was cancelled again.
example.source_literal: Well is, the meeting was cancelled of new.

vocabulary.note: Usage: to manage to sort something out, usually followed by de and an infinitive. Dar is 'to give' and jeito is 'way', 'knack' or 'manner', so the phrase is 'to give a way'. The pattern dar plus a noun is common in Brazilian Portuguese: the noun carries the meaning and dar is the verb that conjugates. Spelling and sound: j is the sound of the s in English 'measure'; ei is one diphthong beat; um is a nasal vowel, with the m only nasalizing it.

example.target: Vou dar um jeito de chegar a tempo.
example.source: I will find a way to arrive on time.
example.source_literal: I-go to-give a way of to-arrive at time.

vocabulary.note: Usage: to watch over something or someone, with the thing watched introduced by em (de olho na panela). Ficar is 'to stay' and de olho is 'of eye', meaning 'with an eye on'. In a casual command the ordinary present form is used (fica, not fique). Spelling and sound: c before a is k; de is said JEE (d before the sound i, which includes a weak final e, becomes j as in jeans); lh is like 'lli' in million; na is em plus a.

example.target: Fica de olho na panela, por favor.
example.source: Keep an eye on the pot, please.
example.source_literal: Stay of eye in-the pot, for favor.

vocabulary.note: Usage: to suffer the consequences of a mistake that was not yours. The image is 'to pay the duck'. The verb pagar conjugates (paguei, pagando) and the rest stays fixed. Spelling and sound: g before a is hard, as in go; in paguei the u is added so that the g stays hard before e; t before o is a plain t; pato is PAH-too.

example.target: Eu não fiz nada e acabei pagando o pato.
example.source: I did nothing and ended up taking the blame.
example.source_literal: I not did nothing and ended paying the duck.

vocabulary.source: to have one's head in the clouds
vocabulary.note: Usage: can mean distracted or very happy, depending on the context. Nas is em plus as, 'in the', so the words say 'to be in the clouds'. Spelling and sound: nuvens ends in ens, a nasal ending that defaults to the second to last syllable, so NU-vens needs no mark; v is as in English. In prêmio, PRÊ-mi-o, the stress is on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, so a mark is written; the e before m is closed, so the circumflex.

example.target: Ela está nas nuvens desde que ganhou o prêmio.
example.source: She has been on cloud nine since she won the prize.
example.source_literal: She is in-the clouds since that she-won the prize.

vocabulary.note: Usage: to be calm or fine with a situation; as a command, Fica de boa means 'take it easy'. Boa is the feminine of bom, 'good', so the words say 'to stay of good'; the feminine noun it stands for is not fixed. Spelling and sound: boa is two syllables, bo-a, because two strong vowels never form a diphthong; the stressed o is open (ó), and no mark is written because the stress falls where the default puts it.

example.target: Pode ficar de boa, eu resolvo isso.
example.source: You can relax, I will handle it.
example.source_literal: Can stay of good, I solve this.

vocabulary.note: Usage: to take someone or something seriously; usually negative (não dar bola). Dar bola para alguém can also mean to show romantic interest. Dar is 'to give' and bola is 'ball'. The command Não dê bola is the negative command of dar, and the circumflex on dê is the one-syllable rule: it separates dê, 'give', from de, 'of'. Spelling and sound: bola has the open ó.

example.target: Não dê bola para o que ele diz.
example.source: Don't pay attention to what he says.
example.source_literal: Not give ball to what he says.

vocabulary.note: Usage: said when something finally sinks in. A ficha was a token that old public telephones needed before they worked. Cair is 'to fall' and the thing that falls is the subject, a ficha, which often stands after the verb. Spelling and sound: ch is sh; cair is ca-IR, two syllables, with no mark because the r shares the syllable of the stressed i; caiu is ca-IU, with no mark because the stressed i shares its syllable with the glide u, and saiu in the dialogues works the same way.

example.target: Só agora caiu a ficha de que eu me formei.
example.source: Only now has it sunk in that I graduated.
example.source_literal: Only now fell the token of that I myself graduated.

vocabulary.source: to cost an arm and a leg
vocabulary.note: Usage: to be very expensive. English uses limbs for the price; Portuguese uses eyes. Da is de plus a, 'of the'. Custar is a regular verb whose subject is the thing bought, so it is nearly always third person (custa, custou, custaram). Spelling and sound: in cus-tar the s closes the syllable, so it is s in São Paulo and sh in Rio; ou is a diphthong, often shortened to a plain closed o; lh in olhos is 'lli' as in million.

example.target: Esse celular custou os olhos da cara.
example.source: This phone cost an arm and a leg.
example.source_literal: This cellphone cost the eyes of-the face.

vocabulary.note: Usage: to put up with something unpleasant without protesting. A sapo is a toad, and the image is of swallowing something distasteful. Spelling and sound: en before a consonant is a nasal vowel, as in tempo; g before o is hard; the final ir is stressed (en-go-LIR), the default for an ending in r; sapo is SAH-poo.

example.target: Tive que engolir sapo no trabalho hoje.
example.source: I had to swallow my pride at work today.
example.source_literal: I-had that swallow toad at-the work today.

vocabulary.target: ficar com a pulga atrás da orelha
vocabulary.source_literal: to-stay with the flea behind of-the ear
vocabulary.note: Usage: to start doubting that something is right. Ficar com is 'to come to have', and the picture is of a flea behind the ear that will not let you rest. Spelling and sound: in pulga the l closes the syllable, so it sounds like w (PUW-ga); atrás is a-TRÁS, stressed on the last syllable although the ending as predicts the second to last, so it has the acute; orelha has lh; fiquei needs qu before e to keep the k sound of ficar.

example.target: Fiquei com a pulga atrás da orelha quando ele mudou de assunto.
example.source: I became suspicious when he changed the subject.
example.source_literal: I-stayed with the flea behind of-the ear when he changed of subject.

vocabulary.note: Usage: describes someone who hates to spend money. The image is 'to be a hand of cow', and the reason for the picture is not transparent. Spelling and sound: mão ends in the nasal ão, which defaults to the last syllable, so the tilde is the only mark needed; v is as in English.

example.target: Meu tio é mão de vaca, nunca paga a conta.
example.source: My uncle is stingy, he never pays the bill.
example.source_literal: My uncle is hand of cow, never pays the bill.

vocabulary.source: to deal with a tough problem
vocabulary.note: Usage: a difficult task or problem is called an abacaxi, 'a pineapple', the usual explanation being that a pineapple is awkward to peel. Descascar is des-, which undoes, plus casca, 'peel': 'to de-peel'. Spelling and sound: des-cas-car is divided des / cas / car, so the s closes a syllable and the c before a is k; this is not the sc of nascer, which is just s. In abacaxi the x says sh, and the stress is on the last syllable, as the ending i predicts.

example.target: Hoje a equipe vai ter que descascar um abacaxi.
example.source: Today the team will have to tackle a tough problem.
example.source_literal: Today the team goes to-have that to-peel a pineapple.

vocabulary.note: Usage: the Northeastern word. The same root vegetable is called mandioca in São Paulo and much of the country, and aipim in Rio and the South; all three words come from Tupi, an indigenous language. Spelling and sound: x between vowels has no rule, and in this word it says sh (ma-ca-SHEI-ra); ei is a diphthong; the stress is on the second to last syllable, so no mark.

example.target: No café da manhã, ela comeu macaxeira com manteiga.
example.source: For breakfast she ate cassava with butter.
example.source_literal: In-the coffee of-the morning she ate cassava with butter.

vocabulary.note: Usage: the word of Rio Grande do Sul. It is called mexerica in São Paulo and Minas Gerais, and tangerina in much of the rest of the country. Spelling and sound: g before a is hard (the hard g of go); the stress is on the second to last syllable, so ber-ga-MO-ta carries no mark; the ending a is a weak uh.

example.target: Os gaúchos comem bergamota no inverno.
example.source: People from Rio Grande do Sul eat tangerines in winter.

vocabulary.note: Usage: the signature interjection of Minas Gerais; it marks surprise or obviousness. It has no literal meaning. Spelling and sound: uai is one syllable, a triphthong, three vowel sounds in one beat (oo-ah-ee, said fast, like the end of Uruguai from the sounds lesson); it ends in i, which defaults to the last syllable, so it needs no mark. The ônibus of the example is Ô-ni-bus, stressed on the third to last syllable, so it always has a mark, the circumflex because the o is closed.

example.target: Uai, você não sabia que o ônibus já saiu?
example.source: Well, didn't you know the bus already left?
example.source_literal: Uai, you not knew that the bus already left?

vocabulary.note: Usage: expresses surprise, fear or admiration; typical of the Northeast. Oxente is a related Northeastern interjection. It has no literal meaning. Spelling and sound: ei is one diphthong beat, so EI-ta has two syllables, stressed on the first, the default for an ending in a, so no mark. In oxente the x says sh: o-XEN-te.

example.target: Eita, que confusão é essa aqui?
example.source: Whoa, what is this mess here?
example.source_literal: Eita, what mess is this here?

vocabulary.note: Usage: the gaúcho interjection, often paired with tchê. It has no literal meaning. Spelling and sound: the final h is silent, as in ah, so bah is said ba. The exclamation que frio is literally 'what cold', meaning 'how cold'.

example.target: Bah, que frio hoje, tchê!
example.source: Gee, it is cold today, mate!
example.source_literal: Bah, what cold today, tchê!

vocabulary.note: Usage: the friendly form of address of Rio Grande do Sul, usually traced to the Spanish che of neighbouring countries. Spelling and sound: tch spells the ch of English cheese, as in tchau. Portuguese ch says sh, and the English ch sound is otherwise only heard as t before i, so tch is written before other vowels. The ê is a stressed one-syllable word ending in e with a closed vowel, so it takes the circumflex.

example.target: Tchê, me passa aquele guri ali.
example.source: Mate, hand me that kid over there.
example.source_literal: Tchê, me pass that boy there.

vocabulary.note: Usage: a mild exclamation of annoyance or surprise, common in São Paulo; avoid it in formal settings. Like pô, it is a softened form of a stronger vulgar word and has no literal meaning. Spelling and sound: tz at the end of a word says ts, as in English cats (PUTS), one syllable; this is not the usual regional s or sh of a final z.

example.target: Putz, esqueci a chave em casa.
example.source: Darn, I left the key at home.
example.source_literal: Putz, I-forgot the key in house.

vocabulary.note: Usage: an invitation to start doing something together, as in Bora trabalhar, let's get to work. It is (vam)os embora, 'let us go away', worn down to its last syllables, and embora alone means 'away'. Spelling and sound: o is the open ó, as in bola; r between vowels is the tap; the stress is on the second to last syllable, so no mark.

example.target: Bora para casa, que já é tarde.
example.source: Let's head home, it's already late.
example.source_literal: Away to house, that already is late.

dialogues.title: Comemorando uma vaga nova
dialogues.context: Three friends in São Paulo talk at a bar after work. Their speech is relaxed and full of fillers.

lines.speaker: Rafa
lines.target: Cara, você viu o jogo ontem? Foi, tipo, a melhor partida do ano.
lines.source: Dude, did you see the game yesterday? It was, like, the best match of the year.
lines.source_literal: Face, you saw the game yesterday? It-was, type, the best match of-the year.

lines.speaker: Léo
lines.target: Não vi, mano. Fiquei preso no trabalho até tarde.
lines.source: I didn't, bro. I was stuck at work until late.
lines.source_literal: Not I-saw, brother. I-stayed stuck in-the work until late.

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.target: Pô, Léo, de novo? Cê tá trabalhando demais, né?
lines.source: Gosh, Léo, again? You're working too much, aren't you?
lines.source_literal: Pô, Léo, of new? You is working too-much, not-is?

lines.speaker: Léo
lines.target: Pois é. Sei lá, acho que meu chefe tá me testando.
lines.source: Yeah. Who knows, I think my boss is testing me.
lines.source_literal: Well is. I-know there, I-think that my boss is me testing.

lines.speaker: Rafa
lines.target: Fica de boa, cara. Você sempre dá um jeito.
lines.source: Take it easy, man. You always find a way.
lines.source_literal: Stay of good, face. You always give a way.

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.target: Eu tô meio nas nuvens hoje. Ontem me ofereceram uma vaga nova e ainda não caiu a ficha.
lines.source: I'm a bit in a daze today. Yesterday they offered me a new position and it still hasn't sunk in.
lines.source_literal: I am half in-the clouds today. Yesterday me they-offered a position new and still not fell the token.

lines.speaker: Léo
lines.target: Nossa, Bia, parabéns! Então vamo comemorar hoje à noite!
lines.source: Wow, Bia, congratulations! Then let's celebrate tonight!
lines.source_literal: Ours, Bia, for-goods! Then we-go to-celebrate today at-the night!

lines.speaker: Rafa
lines.target: Aí sim! Eu conheço uma pizzaria boa e barata aqui perto.
lines.source: Now you're talking! I know a good, cheap pizzeria near here.
lines.source_literal: There yes! I know a pizzeria good and cheap here near.

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.target: Tá bom, mas dessa vez a conta é dividida, né?
lines.source: Okay, but this time we split the bill, right?
lines.source_literal: Is good, but of-this time the bill is divided, not-is?

lines.speaker: Léo
lines.target: Claro. Mas, sei lá, se o Rafa pedir o cardápio inteiro, eu não pago.
lines.source: Of course. But, who knows, if Rafa orders the whole menu, I'm not paying.
lines.source_literal: Clear. But, I-know there, if the Rafa orders the menu whole, I not pay.

dialogues.title: Cada canto com seu nome
dialogues.context: Three colleagues from different regions have lunch at a farm in Minas Gerais and compare what they call the same foods.

lines.speaker: Zé
lines.target: Uai, Marina, vai querer mais um pouco de mandioca frita?
lines.source: Well, Marina, do you want a bit more fried cassava?
lines.source_literal: Uai, Marina, goes to-want more a little of cassava fried?

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.target: Nossa, que delícia! Lá no Rio a gente fala aipim, mas é a mesma coisa, né?
lines.source: Wow, how delicious! In Rio we say aipim, but it's the same thing, right?
lines.source_literal: Ours, what delight! There in-the Rio the people speak aipim, but is the same thing, not-is?

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.target: No Sul também é aipim. E a Tati, lá do Recife, chama de macaxeira.
lines.source: In the South it's aipim too. And Tati, from Recife, calls it macaxeira.
lines.source_literal: In-the South also is aipim. And the Tati, there of-the Recife, calls of macaxeira.

lines.speaker: Zé
lines.target: Uai, cada canto do Brasil tem um nome pra tudo, sô!
lines.source: Well, every corner of Brazil has its own name for everything, man!
lines.source_literal: Uai, each corner of-the Brazil has a name for everything, sir!

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.target: Verdade. Outro dia, no mercado, pedi mexerica e a moça não entendeu nada.
lines.source: True. The other day at the market I asked for mexerica and the woman didn't understand a thing.
lines.source_literal: Truth. Other day, in-the market, I-asked-for mexerica and the young-woman not understood nothing.

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.target: Bah, lá no Sul a gente fala bergamota. Ninguém diz mexerica.
lines.source: Gee, down in the South we say bergamota. Nobody says mexerica.
lines.source_literal: Bah, there in-the South the people speak bergamota. Nobody says mexerica.

lines.speaker: Zé
lines.target: Em Minas é mexerica, mas tem gente que fala tangerina também.
lines.source: In Minas it's mexerica, but some people say tangerina too.
lines.source_literal: In Minas is mexerica, but has people that speak tangerina also.

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.target: Lúcia, lá em Porto Alegre vocês falam tu, não é?
lines.source: Lúcia, in Porto Alegre you use tu, don't you?
lines.source_literal: Lúcia, there in Porto Alegre you-all speak tu, not is?

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.target: Falamos, sim! Lá é tu vai, tu quer, bem solto. Em casa eu ainda falo tchê com os guris.
lines.source: We do! There it's tu vai, tu quer, very relaxed. At home I still say tchê to the kids.
lines.source_literal: We-speak, yes! There is tu goes, tu wants, well loose. In house I still speak tchê with the boys.

lines.speaker: Zé
lines.target: Minha avó chamava tudo de trem: passa o trem pra cá, pega aquele trem ali.
lines.source: My grandmother called everything a trem: pass that thing over here, grab that thing over there.
lines.source_literal: My grandmother called everything of train: pass the train to here, grab that train there.

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.target: Adorei! Agora entendo por que o sotaque de vocês é tão musical.
lines.source: I loved it! Now I understand why your accent is so musical.
lines.source_literal: I-adored! Now I-understand for what the accent of you-all is so musical.

dialogues.title: Depois da apresentação
dialogues.context: A presentation went badly at an advertising agency. Three colleagues talk it over using office idioms.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.target: Pedro, deu tudo errado na apresentação. O cliente ficou com a pulga atrás da orelha.
lines.source: Pedro, everything went wrong in the presentation. The client became suspicious.
lines.source_literal: Pedro, gave everything wrong in-the presentation. The client stayed with the flea behind of-the ear.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.target: Eu sei. E o pior é que eu não fiz nada e acabei pagando o pato.
lines.source: I know. And the worst part is that I did nothing and ended up taking the blame.
lines.source_literal: I know. And the worst is that I not did nothing and ended paying the duck.

lines.speaker: Vera
lines.target: Calma, gente. Vamos dar um jeito. Quem ficou de olho nos números?
lines.source: Calm down, everyone. Let's find a way. Who kept an eye on the numbers?
lines.source_literal: Calm, people. We-go to-give a way. Who stayed of eye in-the numbers?

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.target: Fui eu, mas os dados chegaram errados. Tive que engolir sapo quando o diretor reclamou.
lines.source: It was me, but the data arrived wrong. I had to swallow my pride when the director complained.
lines.source_literal: Was I, but the data arrived wrong. I-had that swallow toad when the director complained.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.target: O programa novo custou os olhos da cara e ainda não funciona direito.
lines.source: The new software cost an arm and a leg and still doesn't work properly.
lines.source_literal: The program new cost the eyes of-the face and still not works right.

lines.speaker: Vera
lines.target: Pois é. E o diretor está nas nuvens, não dá bola para nenhum relatório.
lines.source: Yeah. And the director has his head in the clouds, he doesn't pay attention to any report.
lines.source_literal: Well is. And the director is in-the clouds, not gives ball to no report.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.target: Só agora caiu a ficha de que precisamos refazer tudo até sexta.
lines.source: Only now is it sinking in that we need to redo everything by Friday.
lines.source_literal: Only now fell the token of that we-need to-redo everything until Friday.

lines.speaker: Vera
lines.target: Então mãos à obra. Pedro, você refaz os gráficos, e a Camila fala com o cliente.
lines.source: Then let's get to work. Pedro, you redo the charts, and Camila talks to the client.
lines.source_literal: Then hands to-the work. Pedro, you redo the charts, and the Camila speaks with the client.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.target: Fechado. Mas amanhã eu pago o café, que hoje a coisa tá feia.
lines.source: Deal. But tomorrow I'm buying the coffee, because things look bad today.
lines.source_literal: Closed. But tomorrow I pay the coffee, that today the thing is ugly.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.target: Combinado. Bora trabalhar, que esse abacaxi não se descasca sozinho.
lines.source: Agreed. Let's get to work, because this problem won't solve itself.
lines.source_literal: Combined. Away to-work, for this pineapple not itself peels alone.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: accents and stress in the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Slang and regional words look informal, but they are spelled by the same rules as every other word. The marks in them come out of the procedure from the stress lesson: divide the word into syllables, find the stressed syllable by ear, read the default from the ending, and write an accent only if the stress disagrees with the default. The mark is then chosen by the vowel: the acute for an open vowel (or for i and u, which have only one quality), the circumflex for a closed vowel. The tilde has a different job, which is to make a vowel nasal. Nothing in this unit is marked at random.

The default, restated: words ending in a, e or o (with or without s), am, em or ens are stressed on the second to last syllable, and words ending in anything else, including ã and ão, are stressed on the last. A word that obeys its default needs no mark, which is why most of the slang here is written plainly: tipo is TI-po, cara is CA-ra, eita is EI-ta (ei is one beat), mexerica is me-xe-RI-ca, macaxeira is ma-ca-XEI-ra and bergamota is ber-ga-MO-ta, all stressed on the second to last syllable, while aipim (ai-PIM), guri (gu-RI), abacaxi (a-ba-ca-XI) and uai (one beat) end in i or m and are stressed on the last, as their endings predict.

Group 1, one-syllable words. A word of one syllable has no choice about where the stress falls, so the only question is whether it is stressed or weak. Weak words (de, me, que, um, and the articles a and o) are said lightly, lean on a neighbouring word and carry no mark. The spoken shortenings pra and num are weak in the same way. A stressed one-syllable word that ends in a, e or o (with or without s) is written with a mark: né, pô, lá, tá, tô, cê, sô, dê, tchê, já, é, só, má, and the nickname Zé. This is the whole difference between é (is) and e (and), and between dê (give, in a command) and de (of). The vowel picks the mark: the open vowels of é, né, lá, tá, já and má take the acute, and the closed vowels of pô, tô, cê, sô, dê and tchê take the circumflex. Tá, tô and cê are spoken shortenings, explained in the note on register; once shortened they are simply stressed one-syllable words, so the rule applies to them with no special case.

Group 2, stress on the last syllable although the ending predicts the second to last: atrás (a-TRÁS, ending as) and parabéns (pa-ra-BÉNS, ending ens) take the acute. In parabéns the mark is the acute although the e is nasal, because a word ending in em or ens is marked with an acute by convention. Group 3, a hiatus, which is two vowels that belong to separate syllables. A stressed i or u that stands alone in its syllable after another vowel takes the acute, otherwise the pair would be read as a diphthong. Aí is a-Í: without the mark it would read as ai, the diphthong of pai, and the mark is needed although i at the end of a word defaults to the last syllable. Gaúcho is ga-Ú-cho: without the mark it would be read as gau-cho, and the mark is again about the hiatus and not about the stress. Quase caí is ca-Í for the same reason. No mark is needed when a consonant or glide shares the syllable, which is why cair (ca-IR), caiu (ca-IU) and saiu (sa-IU) have none.

Group 4, stress on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, so a mark is always written: ônibus, números, gráficos, cardápio, específicos, gíria, prêmio, relatório, própria, Lúcia. The vowel decides the mark: ônibus and prêmio have a closed vowel before n or m, so the circumflex; números, gráficos, cardápio, específicos, gíria, relatório, própria and Lúcia have open vowels, or an i or u, which have only one quality, so the acute. The endings ia, io and ios count as two syllables, so the stress of gíria (GÍ-ri-a) and cardápio (car-DÁ-pi-o) is on the third to last. Compare pizzaria, pi-zza-RI-a, where the stressed vowel is the i and the stress is on the second to last syllable, so there is no mark.

Group 5, the tilde endings. The endings ão, ões and ãos default to the last syllable, and the tilde already marks the nasal vowel, so nothing more is written: confusão, expressão, geração, mão, mãos, expressões, então. Last, the grave accent of à in hoje à noite and mãos à obra is the crase of the accents lesson: the preposition a fused with the article a. Names can carry a mark that the rule does not require: Léo shows its open e with an acute although LÉ-o is already stressed where the default puts it.

Worked example, parabéns. Divide it: pa-ra-béns. The stress is by ear on the last syllable. The ending ens defaults to the second to last, so the stress disagrees and a mark is required. The mark is the acute, by the convention for words ending in em and ens. Worked example, gaúcho. Divide it: ga-ú-cho. The stress is on ú, the second to last syllable, which agrees with the default of o; the mark is there only because u is stressed and alone in its syllable after a, which makes a hiatus.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: letters and borrowed spellings in the slang and regional words
grammar.explanation:
The spelling rules of the first lesson predict almost every word in this unit, so the method is to apply them one at a time. The words that look odd fall into a few groups, and each group has a reason. Where a word comes from another language, the spelling follows that language, which is why a few letter combinations do not fit the native rules.

The letters t and d before the sound i. In most of Brazil t becomes ch, as in English cheese, and d becomes j, as in English jeans, before an i or a weak final e (which is said i). So tipo is CHEE-poo, mandioca is man-JEE-O-ka, cidade is see-DAH-jee, de is said jee, and the ending of parte or noite is chee. Before any other vowel they stay plain: pato, sapo, tudo. Some regions, including parts of the Northeast and the far south, keep plain t and d; you are understood either way.

The sound sh has two spellings here. Ch is the ordinary one (ficha, chama, chiado). X is used in a group of words for which the rule is simply to learn each one: macaxeira, mexerica, abacaxi and oxente all have x saying sh, and macaxeira and abacaxi come from Tupi, an indigenous language, as do mandioca and aipim. A separate spelling, tch, is not sh at all; it spells the English ch sound and is borrowed: Portuguese has no native letter for that sound except t before i, so when it occurs before another vowel, as in tchê (and in tchau, goodbye), the spelling tch is used.

The letters c and g, and the spelling changes which keep them steady. Before a, o or u, c is k and g is hard; before e or i, c is s and g is j as in measure. To keep the k sound before e or i you write qu (esqueci, equipe, sotaque), and the u is silent; to keep the hard g before e or i you write gu (guri, guris, paguei). A verb changes its spelling for the same reason: ficar becomes fiquei, because ficei would be read fi-SAY. To keep an s sound before a, o or u you write ç (moça, conheçam). A letter c before i is s (delícia, aparecia), and g before e or i is j (tangerina, gíria, geração), while bergamota, with g before a, keeps the hard g. In descascar the pair s and c is not the sc of nascer and adolescente, which says a single s before e or i: here s ends one syllable (des) and c begins the next (cas), and before a the c says k.

Sounds that depend on position. The letter l at the end of a syllable sounds like w (PUW-ga, Sul). The letter s at the end of a syllable follows the region: s in São Paulo and much of the south and centre, sh in the city of Rio de Janeiro, so pois and custou carry the chiado of Rio. Ss between vowels is a single s (nossa). The strong r is written r at the start of a word (Rio, Recife, refazer) and rr between vowels (errados). The tap is written r between vowels (cara, carioca, hora). Finally, nasal vowels are written with a tilde or with m or n after the vowel, before a consonant or at the end of a word (canto, mandioca, mundos, engolir, aipim), and the endings ão and ões are stressed and nasal (mão, confusão, expressões), while ens is a nasal ending (nuvens). The word uai is a triphthong, three vowel sounds in one beat.

Borrowed letters. Putz ends in tz, which says ts, as in English cats; the same ts is written zz in pizzaria, from Italian. Funk keeps its English spelling, and Brazilians add a light i after the final k. Skatistas and surfistas keep their English roots, sk and surf. By itself h is always silent, in hoje and in the final h of bah (in ch, lh and nh it belongs to a pair). Finally, the weak unstressed vowels of the first lesson apply to every word here: final a is a short uh, final o is u and final e is i, so pato is PAH-too and sapo is SAH-poo.

grammar.title: Discourse markers in everyday speech
grammar.explanation:
Discourse is connected speech, more than one sentence talking about one subject. A discourse marker is a small word whose job is not to add information but to organize the talk: to open an idea, soften a statement, ask for agreement, show the speaker's attitude or signal a change of topic. A filler is a marker used to fill a pause or to give the speaker time. English has them too (well, so, like, you know, right?, man), and English speakers use them without noticing. Portuguese markers are built the same way: an ordinary word loses most of its literal meaning and takes a job in organizing speech. What matters is therefore the function, and the literal meaning is a clue to where the function came from.

Tipo was the noun 'type' and now introduces an example or hedges. Né is não é, 'not is', and ends a statement to ask for agreement. English changes its tag question with the verb and the polarity (isn't it, don't you, can't they), but Portuguese uses one invariable tag, né, or the full não é, whatever the sentence. Aí is the adverb 'there' and now moves a story forward, the everyday replacement for então or depois in narration. Então is 'then' and restarts or wraps up a point. Pois é, 'well is', agrees or concedes. Sei lá, 'I-know there', expresses doubt or indifference. É isso, 'is that', closes a thought. Tá is a shortened está and means 'okay'.

Cara, mano and pô are a different type. Cara and mano are vocatives, which means words used to address someone directly: cara is literally 'face' and mano is 'brother', and both now mean roughly 'dude' and 'bro' and are used between friends of any gender. Pô is an interjection, a word that expresses a feeling and has no grammar. It is a softened form of a stronger vulgar word, and that is why it is informal but harmless. Markers are often said lightly and quickly.

In writing, in interviews and in meetings with people you do not know, use them very sparingly. Overusing tipo and né sounds careless in formal contexts, but using none at all sounds stiff among friends. The table lists each marker with its literal source, its job and its closest English.

grammar.title: Regional variation: vocabulary, accents and tu versus você
grammar.explanation:
Brazilian Portuguese is remarkably uniform in writing, but speech changes from region to region on three separate levels: accent (the sounds), vocabulary (the words) and grammar (the pronoun tu and the verb forms that go with it). A regional variety of a language is called a dialect, and Brazilians usually place each other's region within a sentence or two. The differences exist because the language met different languages in different places: Tupi and other indigenous languages supplied the names of plants and animals (mandioca, aipim, macaxeira, abacaxi), African languages left words, and immigrant communities in the south and southeast shaped local speech. English has the same situation, with lift and elevator, or boot and trunk.

Accent. The carioca accent (Rio de Janeiro) says a syllable-final s as sh (this sh is called the chiado) and uses mermão. The paulistano accent (São Paulo) says it as s and uses mano and meu, which is literally 'my' but is used to address a friend, like 'dude'. In the countryside of São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Goiás, the r at the end of a syllable is an American-style r (the so-called R caipira). In Minas Gerais speakers swallow unstressed syllables, say uai and sô (a reduction of senhor, 'sir'), and use trem for 'thing'. In the Northeast the unstressed vowels stay open and clear, which is heard as musical, and t and d often stay plain before i; eita and oxente are typical. In the South, especially Rio Grande do Sul, bah and tchê are frequent, and guri and guria mean boy and girl.

Vocabulary. Names for foods are the standard example, and the table shows them. Nothing is wrong with any of these: each is standard in its own region, and the only risk is that an attendant from another region will not understand.

Grammar: tu versus você. Tu is the second person singular pronoun, 'you' to one person. In most of Brazil the speaker uses você with a third person verb. Tu is normal in parts of the North, the Northeast, Rio Grande do Sul and Florianópolis. There are two ways to use it. The textbook way takes the second person verb form, which ends in s: tu falas, tu queres, tu vais. The way heard most often in speech takes the third person form, exactly as você does: tu fala, tu quer, tu vai. Both are real, and neither changes the meaning. As a learner, você is always safe, and you will understand tu when you hear it.

grammar.title: Idioms with animals, food and body parts
grammar.explanation:
An idiom is a fixed phrase whose meaning belongs to the whole phrase and cannot be worked out from the words. English has them (kick the bucket, spill the beans), and nobody hears a bucket or beans. This course keeps three things apart for each idiom: the words, word for word, in the field called literal; the natural English equivalent, in the translation; and the usage, in the notes. The literal meaning is worth reading because it shows the image the idiom is built on, and the images differ from English on purpose. Portuguese counts the price in eyes where English counts limbs (custar os olhos da cara, 'to cost the eyes of the face', against 'an arm and a leg'), and the penny that drops in English is a token that falls in Portuguese (cair a ficha), two images that come from coin-operated machines, a slot machine and a public telephone.

The usual pattern in an idiom is that the verb is free and the rest is frozen, within what the meaning allows: custar and cair, for example, almost always have a third person subject. The verb conjugates for person, tense and mood like any other verb (pagar o pato, paguei o pato, vamos pagar o pato), but the noun phrase does not change: the duck stays a duck, and the article and the noun cannot be replaced or pluralized without losing the idiom. Some idioms carry a contraction that you should recognize rather than analyze: estar nas nuvens contains nas, which is em plus as, and custar os olhos da cara contains da, which is de plus a. In cair a ficha the thing that falls, a ficha, is the subject and often stands after the verb, so the person who understands is not named at all. Three constructions recur. Acabar plus the gerund (the -ndo form) means 'to end up doing': acabei pagando o pato, 'I ended up paying the duck'. Ter que plus an infinitive means 'to have to': tive que engolir sapo. Viver plus the gerund means 'to keep doing something all the time': ele vive engolindo sapo.

Two verbs carry a large share of Brazilian idioms, and their plain meanings explain why. Dar is 'to give', and in a pattern dar plus noun the noun carries the meaning while dar is the verb that conjugates: dar um jeito (give a way), dar bola (give ball), dar uma força (give a strength, meaning to help). Ficar is 'to stay' or 'to become', and the small word after it says what you stay in: ficar de olho (stay of eye, that is, keeping watch), ficar de boa (stay of good), ficar com a pulga atrás da orelha (stay with the flea behind the ear). Ficar com plus a noun means to come to have it, and ficar de plus a noun phrase means to be in that position. In the preterite, ficar writes qu before e to keep the k sound, so fiquei.

The idioms in this unit are informal but not vulgar. You can use them in relaxed conversation with colleagues, but in formal writing it is better to use a plain equivalent, such as prestar atenção instead of dar bola, or ser avarento instead of ser mão de vaca. grammar.title: Register: slang, vulgarity and spoken shortenings
grammar.explanation:
Register is the level of formality a speaker chooses for a situation. Brazilian Portuguese has three layers. Gíria (slang) is informal but harmless: tipo, mano, de boa, bora. Palavrão (vulgar language) is offensive and should be avoided by learners until the context is completely clear. Formal register is used for writing, work and official situations. The same message changes word choice with the register: dar bola in a chat, prestar atenção in a report. Choosing the right one matters more than knowing the word.

Spoken shortenings follow one principle: in fast speech Portuguese weakens or drops syllables that carry little stress, and the writer of informal text writes what is heard. Está loses its unstressed first syllable and becomes tá; estou loses it and becomes tô; você loses vo- and becomes cê; para, a weak word, loses the a after p and becomes pra, and para o becomes pro; vamos loses its final s and becomes vamo; não before a verb, said weakly, becomes num; não é becomes né; and vamos embora wears down to bora. None of these is an error, and all are standard among native speakers, but they are not written in formal texts. Pra, tá and né appear often in informal writing, such as messages and social media, but never in a letter to a company.

Because the shortened forms are new words, the stress rules of the accents lesson apply to them. Tá, tô and cê are stressed one-syllable words ending in a, o or e, so they take a mark, chosen by the vowel: the open a of tá takes the acute, and the closed o and e of tô and cê take the circumflex. Pra and num are weak, so they have no mark. Num also has a second life that must not be confused with it: num is the contraction of em plus um, 'in a', as in num prédio, and only the context tells them apart: before a verb it is não, before a noun it is em plus um.

A practical rule: match the register of the person you are talking to. When in doubt, use the plain full form. It is never rude to speak slightly more formally than needed, but slang in the wrong place can be awkward.

grammar.title: Phrases in the dialogues: literal meaning and use
grammar.explanation:
Several short phrases in the dialogues are fixed chunks, and each has a literal meaning, a natural English equivalent and a use, which differ. They are set apart here so that you can read the words as they are and still know what the speaker means.

Nossa is literally 'ours' (feminine). It began as the first word of Nossa Senhora, 'Our Lady', and is now only a way to show surprise or admiration, with no religious sense, as English 'gosh' began as a form of 'God'. Parabéns is para, 'for', plus bens, 'goods', so 'for goods', and is always plural; it is said to someone who has done something well. Aí sim is 'there yes' and approves of a plan: 'now you're talking'. Mãos à obra is 'hands to the work', an urge to start; mãos is the plural of mão, and à is a plus a. Deu tudo errado is literally 'gave everything wrong': dar is used in the sense of turning out, so dar certo is to work out and dar errado is to go wrong. Tô meio nas nuvens uses meio, 'half', as an adverb meaning 'somewhat'; it does not change for gender. A conta é dividida is 'the bill is divided', a passive with ser: ser plus the participle, with the bill as the subject. Que in a hoje a coisa tá feia is 'because', not 'that': 'because today the thing is ugly', meaning 'things look bad'. A coisa, 'the thing', is the everyday word for the situation.

Regional words appear as themselves. Sô is a Minas reduction of senhor, 'sir', used to any listener; the Minas word trem means train and also 'thing', so passa o trem is 'pass the train' and means 'pass that thing'. A moça is a young woman, and the word is often used for a female shop attendant. Guris is the plural of guri, 'boy' in Rio Grande do Sul, so 'os guris' is the kids. Não entendeu nada is 'did not understand nothing', with a double negation: Portuguese puts não before the verb and nada after it, and the two do not cancel each other as they would in standard English. Lá no Sul is 'there in the South', and lá adds distance and emphasis. Outro dia is 'other day' and means 'the other day'. A gente fala aipim is literally 'the people speak aipim', and means 'we say aipim', with a gente taking a third person singular verb, as in the pronouns lesson. Cada canto is 'each corner', meaning 'every place'.

Two more chunks. Fechado, 'closed', and combinado, 'combined', are participles used as replies, 'deal' and 'agreed'; they are the same chunks as in the earlier lesson on the future subjunctive. Bora is the end of vamos embora, explained in the note on register. Claro is 'clear' and means 'of course': what is clear needs no argument.

culture.title: O sotaque como identidade
culture.text:
In Brazil an accent, or sotaque, is a strong marker of identity, and it is also a source of humor and affection. People from Rio are known for the chiado, the sh sound at the end of syllables; the word comes from a verb for hissing. Paulistanos are teased for saying meu (literally 'my', used like 'dude') and mano, and for the so-called R caipira of the countryside of São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Goiás, an r at the end of a syllable that sounds like the American r. The Northeast is admired for its rhythm and its colorful interjections. Gaúchos are recognized by bah, tchê and their tu forms.

For decades, television newscasts tried to create a neutral accent, which is why national anchors sounded almost regionless. Today that is changing: streaming series, podcasts and social media give space to real local speech, and expressions such as uai, oxente and bah have spread across the country. Still, prejudice against some accents exists, especially toward the Northeast and the rural interior, and many people change their speech when they move to another city.

For a learner, the best approach is to listen widely and to be flexible. Brazilians generally appreciate any effort to speak their language, and asking 'Como vocês chamam isso aqui?', literally 'how you-all call this here?', is a very good conversation starter. Be careful with slang that sounds too local or too crude: it is better to understand it than to imitate it right away.

paragraphs.target: Quando Juliana saiu de Recife para morar em Porto Alegre, achou que a mudança seria apenas de cidade. Logo no primeiro dia, porém, percebeu que teria de aprender uma nova língua dentro da própria língua.
paragraphs.source: When Juliana left Recife to live in Porto Alegre, she thought the change would be only one of city. On the very first day, however, she realized she would have to learn a new language inside her own language.

paragraphs.target: No mercado, pediu macaxeira e a atendente olhou para ela sem entender. Depois de rir um pouco, a moça explicou que ali se dizia aipim.
paragraphs.source: At the market she asked for macaxeira and the attendant looked at her without understanding. After laughing a little, the woman explained that there they said aipim.

paragraphs.target: Nas semanas seguintes, as surpresas continuaram. Os colegas da faculdade diziam bah e tchê a cada frase, e a palavra guri aparecia o tempo todo para falar de menino.
paragraphs.source: In the following weeks, the surprises continued. Her college classmates said bah and tchê in every sentence, and the word guri appeared all the time to mean boy.

paragraphs.target: Juliana, que sempre dizia oxente quando ficava espantada, descobriu que ninguém entendia a expressão. Por outro lado, todos adoravam o jeito cantado com que ela falava.
paragraphs.source: Juliana, who had always said oxente when she was astonished, discovered that nobody understood the expression. On the other hand, everybody loved the singsong way she spoke.
paragraphs.source_literal: Juliana, who always said oxente when she-stayed astonished, discovered that nobody understood the expression. For other side, everyone adored the way sung with which she spoke.

paragraphs.target: Com o tempo, ela aprendeu a misturar os dois mundos. Hoje diz bergamota em vez de tangerina quando está no Sul, mas continua dizendo macaxeira quando liga para a mãe.
paragraphs.source: With time she learned to mix the two worlds. Today she says bergamota instead of tangerina when she is in the South, but she keeps saying macaxeira when she calls her mother.

paragraphs.target: Quando volta a Recife, os amigos brincam que ela está falando gaúcho. Juliana responde que não há problema: um sotaque não se perde, só ganha mais camadas.
paragraphs.source: When she goes back to Recife, her friends joke that she is speaking gaúcho. Juliana answers that this is no problem: an accent is not lost, it just gains more layers.
paragraphs.source_literal: When she-returns to Recife, the friends joke that she is speaking gaúcho. Juliana answers that not there-is problem: an accent not itself loses, only gains more layers.

readings.title: Por que a gíria muda tão rápido?

paragraphs.target: A gíria é a parte da língua que mais rapidamente se transforma.
paragraphs.source: Slang is the part of language that changes most quickly.

paragraphs.target: Nos anos noventa, muita gente dizia que algo era maneiro ou irado; hoje, os jovens preferem expressões diferentes, e essas palavras já soam antigas para eles.
paragraphs.source: In the nineties many people said something was maneiro or irado; today young people prefer different expressions, and those words already sound old to them.

paragraphs.target: Por isso, quem aprende português pela televisão ou por músicas antigas pode acabar falando como uma geração passada.
paragraphs.source: For this reason, someone who learns Portuguese from television or old songs may end up speaking like a past generation.

paragraphs.target: Muitas gírias nascem em grupos específicos, como torcidas de futebol, comunidades do funk, surfistas e skatistas, e depois se espalham pelas redes sociais.
paragraphs.source: Many slang words are born in specific groups, such as soccer fan clubs, funk communities, surfers and skaters, and then spread through social media.

paragraphs.target: Quando uma expressão chega à televisão e à publicidade, os jovens já estão procurando outra.
paragraphs.source: When an expression reaches television and advertising, young people are already looking for another one.

paragraphs.target: Esse movimento constante explica por que falar como um adolescente costuma parecer forçado para quem já passou dessa idade.
paragraphs.source: This constant movement explains why talking like a teenager usually seems forced for someone who is past that age.
paragraphs.source_literal: This movement constant explains for what to-speak like a teenager is-accustomed to-seem forced for who already passed of-this age.

paragraphs.target: Os linguistas lembram que gíria não é erro. É uma escolha de registro: entre amigos ela cria proximidade, mas em uma entrevista de emprego pode causar má impressão.
paragraphs.source: Linguists point out that slang is not a mistake. It is a choice of register: among friends it creates closeness, but in a job interview it can make a bad impression.

paragraphs.target: Também é preciso distinguir a gíria do palavrão. A primeira é informal, porém em geral inofensiva; o segundo é ofensivo e deve ser evitado por estrangeiros até que conheçam bem o contexto.
paragraphs.source: It is also necessary to distinguish slang from swearing. The first is informal but generally harmless; the second is offensive and should be avoided by foreigners until they know the context well.

exercises.prompt: Why is né written with an accent?
choices: It is a stressed one-syllable word ending in e, and the vowel is open
It ends in a nasal vowel
It is stressed on the third to last syllable
exercises.explanation: A stressed one-syllable word ending in a, e or o is written with a mark. The open vowel takes the acute. The weak word e, 'and', is unmarked.

exercises.prompt: How is the t pronounced in tipo?
exercises.explanation: In most of Brazil t becomes ch before the sound i, so tipo is CHEE-poo.

exercises.prompt: Word for word, what does cair a ficha say?
exercises.explanation: Cair is 'to fall' and a ficha is the token for an old public telephone. The natural meaning, for something to sink in, is separate from the words.

exercises.prompt: Why does gaúcho have an accent on the ú?
choices: Because the word is stressed on the last syllable
Because the accent keeps a and u in separate syllables instead of a diphthong
Because the word comes from Spanish
exercises.explanation: Ga-Ú-cho is stressed where the default puts it, so the mark is not about the stress. It shows a hiatus: without it the letters would be read as the diphthong au.

exercises.prompt: In pagar o pato, which part changes with the subject and the tense?
exercises.explanation: In an idiom the verb conjugates (paguei o pato, pagando o pato) and the noun phrase stays fixed.

exercises.prompt: Which reply is best in a formal meeting with a client?

exercises.explanation: The full, polite form suits a formal register; the others are slang.

exercises.prompt: In Ele mora num prédio novo, what is num?
choices: The contraction of em plus um
exercises.explanation: Num before a verb is não, but here it comes before a noun, where it is em plus um, 'in a'.

exercises.prompt: English changes its tag question with the verb (isn't it, don't you). What does Portuguese do with né?
choices: It changes né with the verb
It uses né only after questions
It uses one invariable tag at the end of any statement
It uses né only with ser
exercises.explanation: Né is não é, 'not is', used after any statement whatever the verb.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence uses tu with the textbook verb form?
exercises.explanation: The textbook second person singular ends in s: tu queres. Tu quer, with the third person form, is common in speech but is not the textbook form.

exercises.prompt: How is the l pronounced in pulga?
choices: Like w, the end of now
exercises.explanation: An l at the end of a syllable sounds like w, so pulga is PUW-ga.

exercises.prompt: Which word do people in Recife use for mandioca?
exercises.explanation: Macaxeira is the Northeastern word; aipim is used in Rio and the South.

exercises.prompt: Which interjection is most typical of Minas Gerais?
exercises.explanation: Uai is the signature interjection of Minas; bah is gaúcho and eita is Northeastern.

exercises.hint_source: This car cost an arm and a leg.
exercises.explanation: Da is de plus a: 'of the face'. The noun cara is feminine, so the article is a and it fuses with de.

exercises.hint_source: She has been in the clouds since yesterday.
exercises.explanation: Nas is em plus as: 'in the clouds'. Nuvens is plural and feminine.

exercises.hint_source: It is cold today, isn't it? Use the one-word spoken form of não é.
exercises.explanation: Né is the colloquial tag question, from não é.

exercises.prompt_target: Ontem eu ___ de olho nas crianças a tarde toda.
exercises.hint_source: Yesterday I kept an eye on the kids all afternoon. Use ficar.
exercises.explanation: The first person preterite of ficar is fiquei: c becomes qu before e so that the k sound stays.
The negative command of dar is dê. The circumflex separates dê, 'give', from the weak word de, 'of'. In casual speech the present form dá is also used as a command.
Para loses its first syllable in speech and becomes pra.

exercises.prompt_target: Só agora ___ a ficha de que ele foi embora.
exercises.hint_source: Only now has it sunk in that he left.
exercises.explanation: The subject is a ficha, after the verb. The event has just happened, so the preterite caiu is used; it has no accent because the stressed i shares its syllable with u.
